reconcile.connective: Commentators read Priscilla's instruction of Apollos as private, household teaching, distinct from the public church-teaching-of-men the epistles restrict.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the same silencing of women as evidence 1 Timothy is pseudonymous: the undisputed Paul's own 'no male and female' (Galatians 3:28) cuts the other way, so a letter ordering women to keep silent reads to him as a later forger's hand, not Paul's.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Forged: Writing in the Name of God

excerpts.excerpt_text: Here is an instance of a good woman, though not permitted to speak in the church or in the synagogue, yet doing good with the knowledge God had given her in private converse.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Matthew Henry's closing observation on the Priscilla/Apollos episode states the standard harmonizing mechanism directly: Priscilla's instruction of Apollos was private ('in private converse'), not the public church-speech 1 Cor 14:34-35/1 Tim 2:11-12 restrict — the note is keyed to Acts 18:24 sequentially but its own 'cites' this row's Acts 18:26.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley's "Ethical Discrepancies" chapter (pp. 309-311) prints this row's exact three verses side by side under the heading "Must keep silence. / May prophesy and teach" — 1 Cor 14:34-35 and 1 Tim 2:11-12 quoted on the left, Acts 18:26 (Priscilla and Aquila expounding "the way of God more perfectly" to Apollos) among the right-column texts. Haley argues the silencing texts were prudent, local counsel tied to Corinth's and Ephesus's notorious immodesty rather than a universal, timeless rule, citing Conybeare on Corinth's "peculiar licentiousness," Neander, and Adam Clarke's view that Paul restricts public disputing/dictating, not all speech.
